trend_source: A Canadian creator's video splitting a $5,000 salary into 55/5/10/15/15 pulled 365.9k views, 6.8k likes and 2.1k shares, proving simple paycheck-splitting frameworks travel well.
title: The percentage split I'd use on a Singapore paycheck
hooks: If your pay hits your account and vanishes by the 20th, you don't have a money problem, you have a plan problem.
Here is one simple way to give every dollar of your salary a job before you spend it.
I make my clients split their pay into five buckets, and most feel in control within a month.
talking_points: 55% for essentials: HDB or rent, utilities, groceries, transport
5% guilt-free spending so the plan is sustainable, plus 15% for short-term goals like a holiday
10% to clear debt first, or redirect to investing if you are debt-free
15% for long-term wealth: topping up CPF, SRS or an investment plan you review yearly
cta: Comment SPLIT and I'll send you a Singapore version of this breakdown you can adjust to your own salary.
why_it_works: The format is already proven across borders and feels doable rather than preachy, so localising the buckets to CPF and SRS adds real value without hijacking the hook.
how_to_film: Talk straight to camera, hold up five fingers and count down each bucket. Open with the vanishing-paycheck line. Keep it brisk, one bucket per breath, and end on the CPF/SRS point.
author: @jordfinance

trend_source: A US creator's 'how I'd invest my first $1,000' video hit 80.8k views and 6.8k likes by keeping beginner investing simple, though his picks are US-specific funds.
title: Investing your first $1,000 in Singapore without overthinking it
hooks: You do not need to pick the perfect stock to start investing, you need to start.
If I had $1,000 and was starting over in Singapore, here's how I'd keep it stupidly simple.
Everyone asks me which share to buy first, and that's exactly the wrong first question.
talking_points: US videos name specific American funds, which don't apply here; focus on the principle of broad diversification instead
Spreading money across many companies and regions lowers the chance one bad bet wrecks you
Decide your time horizon and how much ups and downs you can stomach before you buy anything
Automate a monthly amount so you keep investing through good and bad markets
cta: DM me BEGINNER and I'll walk you through building a simple first portfolio that fits your goals and risk comfort.
why_it_works: Beginners crave a clear first step, and correcting the US-fund specifics into a Singapore-appropriate principle is more honest and more useful than repeating foreign tickers.
how_to_film: Casual, phone-at-arm's-length. Open with 'you do not need the perfect stock'. Count the principles on screen as text overlays. Slow down on the diversification point.

trend_source: A savings-planner video on breaking a $5,000 goal into per-paycheck chunks drew 444.5k views and 379 shares, showing people love goals that feel small enough to hit.
title: How to actually save $5,000 without feeling the pinch
hooks: Saving $5,000 sounds scary until you see it's about $100 a week.
A big savings goal feels impossible because you're staring at the whole mountain at once.
Here's the maths trick that makes a $5,000 goal feel boring instead of overwhelming.
talking_points: Pick the deadline, then divide the target by the number of paydays to get a per-paycheck amount
Set up an automatic transfer on payday so you never see the money as spendable
Keep the savings in a separate account so it's out of sight and harder to raid
Name the goal (emergency fund, wedding, down payment) so you stay motivated to protect it
cta: Save this and tell me in the comments what you're saving $5,000 for.
why_it_works: The chunking idea is universal and already viral; it earns attention by making a daunting goal feel achievable, which is honest motivational planning.
how_to_film: Write the maths on a whiteboard or screen text: $5,000 divided by weeks. Open with the $100-a-week line. Point to the numbers as you talk, upbeat pace.

trend_source: A US creator who cleared $90k of debt shared her 90-day plan to 15.8k views, 2k likes and 183 comments, proving tactical debt stories resonate.
title: The first 90 days I'd spend attacking credit card debt
hooks: The reason your card balance never moves isn't you, it's the interest compounding faster than you pay.
If I had to clear credit card debt in Singapore starting today, here's my first 90 days.
Stop telling me you keep the card for the rewards, the interest is eating those alive.
talking_points: Stop adding to the card and switch to a weekly cash or debit budget so spending stops when the money does
Call the bank and ask about hardship or restructuring options instead of ignoring statements
Look into balance transfer or consolidation to reduce the interest dragging you down (check the real terms first)
Funnel every extra dollar of income straight at the smallest or highest-interest balance
cta: Book a free chat and we'll map out your personal debt-clearing plan before interest adds another cent.
why_it_works: A concrete debt-payoff playbook earns trust, and adapting the US tactics (balance transfers, hardship calls) to Singapore keeps it honest and actionable.
how_to_film: Direct, slightly urgent tone. Open with the compounding-interest line. List steps as numbered captions. Keep energy high but reassuring, not fear-mongering.

trend_source: A US creator's 'what I'd do if the market keeps dropping' video reached 35.3k views and 1.2k likes, showing appetite for calm-in-a-downturn content.
title: Three calm moves when the market is falling
hooks: When the market drops, panic is the most expensive emotion you can act on.
If markets keep sliding, here are three things I'd do with my money, and none of them is panic-sell.
The investors who get rich in a downturn are usually the ones who did nothing dramatic.
talking_points: Keep your emergency cash somewhere stable and accessible so a dip never forces you to sell at a loss
Tighten the budget and trim subscriptions you forgot you had to free up cash
Keep investing steadily; downturns are when disciplined investors buy at lower prices
Avoid timing the bottom; focus on your time horizon and your plan instead
cta: Comment CALM and I'll share a simple checklist for staying steady when markets get noisy.
why_it_works: Downturn anxiety is real and recurring, and offering composure plus a plan is honest value rather than the fear-selling many finance clips lean on.
how_to_film: Calm, measured voice, seated. Open with the panic line. Use three fingers for the three moves. Let the 'do nothing dramatic' point land with a pause.

title: The quiet money habit behind the first-class seat
hooks: Everyone dreams of the suites in the sky, but almost nobody plans for how to actually afford them.
A luxury flight looks effortless, but the money behind it rarely is.
You don't need to win the lottery to fly up front one day, you need a sinking fund.
talking_points: Big-ticket experiences come from planning, not luck; a dedicated 'experiences' savings pot makes them real
Separate your wants-fund from your needs so treating yourself doesn't wreck your goals
Automate a small monthly amount toward the splurge you actually care about
Protect the plan first: emergency fund and insurance before luxury, so one setback doesn't undo years of saving
cta: Comment DREAM and tell me the one splurge you'd save a sinking fund for.
why_it_works: The aspirational flight grabs attention honestly, and pivoting to 'how dreams get funded' turns envy into a useful planning conversation without shaming anyone.
how_to_film: Film against a travel or window backdrop. Open with the suites-in-the-sky line. Keep it warm and relatable, land on the 'protect the plan first' point.

trend_source: The Financial Coconut's story of a $300,000 cancer bill and its hidden extras reached 45.4k views, about 7.1x their usual, citing a Prudential poll on critical illness costs.
title: The cancer costs that never show up on the hospital bill
hooks: The $300,000 hospital bill was only part of what his cancer actually cost.
People plan for the hospital bill and forget everything else that drains the bank account.
TCM, special meals, transport, a massage chair: the costs of illness don't stop at the ward door.
talking_points: Insurance often covers the hospital bill, but recovery brings extra costs that come straight from savings
Think transport to appointments, dietary changes, alternative therapies and lost income during recovery
A critical illness payout is designed to cover living and recovery costs, not just treatment
Review your coverage against what recovery actually costs, not just the headline hospital figure
cta: DM me GAP for a simple way to check whether your coverage accounts for the hidden costs of illness.
why_it_works: It's a locally produced video citing a real Singapore poll, and the hidden-cost angle is an honest, non-fear way to explain what critical illness cover is for.
how_to_film: Calm, sincere tone, seated close to camera. Open with the $300k line. List the hidden costs as on-screen text. Avoid dramatics; let the facts carry weight.

trend_source: A Chinese-language reel on a five-figure earner left with $1 in the bank drew 15.7k views, about 5.1x the creator's usual, hitting the earning-versus-keeping nerve.
title: Earning a lot and keeping nothing are two different skills
hooks: I've met people earning five figures a month with almost nothing in the bank.
A high income does not make you rich, your savings do.
The scariest money story I know is the person who earns a lot and keeps none of it.
talking_points: Lifestyle upgrades expand to swallow a rising income if you have no plan
Rent, bills and insurance keep coming even when your income dips, so a buffer matters
Earning money is one skill; keeping it is a harder, more valuable one
Pay yourself first by saving and protecting before you upgrade your lifestyle
cta: Open question for you: do you agree that keeping money is harder than making it?
why_it_works: The real local story of a high earner going broke makes the earning-versus-keeping point land emotionally, and the lesson is honest and widely relatable.
how_to_film: Conversational, reflective tone. Open with the five-figures-and-nothing line. Pace slowly so the lesson sinks in. End by genuinely inviting the audience's take.
